You previously formulated the following research problem for the target paper.

Research problem: When MVFA is transferred to a new modality, can its multi-level adapters be adapted using only an unlabelled batch of target images — no masks, no image-level labels and no curated normal support set — by transductive self-training on its own zero-shot anomaly maps, and does this close the gap between MVFA's zero-shot and few-shot performance? Concretely: starting from the source-trained zero-shot MVFA, generate pixel pseudo-labels on N unlabelled target images from confident regions of the zero-shot anomaly maps (very low scores as normal, very high scores as abnormal, the rest ignored), fine-tune only the adapters with the original segmentation-alignment losses restricted to confident pixels for a small number of rounds, and measure image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on a disjoint target test split as a function of N and of the confidence thresholds, against zero-shot MVFA and against few-shot MVFA with K labelled images.
Rationale: MVFA's few-shot mode assumes K target images that are labelled, include abnormal cases and come with masks (G4), while its training assumes dense masks on the source data (G3). A common clinical reality is different: a hospital deploying the model has many unlabelled scans from the new scanner or modality, but no annotation budget. The related work shows that pseudo-labels from CLIP can refine anomaly localisation — AnoCLIP uses a test-time adaptation step with its own pseudo-labels for industrial images — but this has not been studied for multi-level medical adapters, where a wrong pseudo-label on an unseen modality could reinforce errors, and where the relevant comparison is with labelled few-shot adaptation. This differs from training with image-level labels: here the target modality has no labels of any kind, and the question is whether self-generated supervision is reliable enough under modality shift. It changes only the adaptation data and loss mask in the public MVFA code, runs on one GPU, and its risks (confirmation bias) are measurable through the curves over N and thresholds. The modality-disjoint protocol is essential, since pseudo-labelling an OCT dataset after training on the other OCT dataset would not test transfer at all.

ReviewingAgents evaluated it on five criteria. Their reviews, feedback, and ratings are:
- Clarity: rating 4/5. Review: The setting (unlabelled target batch, pseudo-labels from confident regions, adapters only, confident-pixel losses) and outcomes (AUROC, PRO as functions of N and thresholds, versus zero-shot and few-shot MVFA) are clearly stated. Feedback: Define how the target data is split into the unlabelled adaptation pool and the disjoint test set for each BMAD modality, since some BMAD test sets are small, and define the confidence thresholds (quantiles of the zero-shot scores) up front.
- Relevance: rating 4/5. Review: Unlabelled target data under modality shift is a realistic deployment condition and connects to G4. The problem is well connected to AnoCLIP's test-time adaptation and to MVFA's zero-/few-shot comparison. Feedback: Relate it to source-free domain adaptation, which is the established name for this setting.
- Originality: rating 3/5. Review: Self-training on pseudo-labels and test-time adaptation are standard; AnoCLIP already performs pseudo-label adaptation for CLIP-based localisation. Moving it to multi-level medical adapters and studying confirmation bias under modality shift adds some insight but the core idea is familiar. Feedback: Identify an element that is specific to the medical, multi-level setting — for example, using agreement across the four feature levels as the confidence criterion — to differentiate the problem from generic self-training.
- Feasibility: rating 4/5. Review: Implementable in the MVFA code and cheap to run, but several BMAD modalities have few test images, so carving out an unlabelled adaptation pool reduces the test set and widens confidence intervals; pseudo-label quality on modalities where zero-shot AUROC is already low (e.g., chest X-ray) may be too poor to bootstrap. Feedback: Report how the adaptation/test split interacts with variance, and include a modality with weak zero-shot performance as a stress test.
- Significance: rating 3/5. Review: Useful for deployment, but the expected outcome is an incremental shift along the zero-shot/few-shot continuum; it does not change what supervision MVFA needs for its source training (G3), which is the larger barrier. Feedback: Clarify what decision a clinic could make from the result (e.g., how many unlabelled scans are needed to match K labelled ones).

Revise the research problem so that it addresses the feedback while keeping what the reviewers rated highly. Keep it a single, fine-grained, to-the-point problem that still addresses the same limitations, respects the constraints below, and stays centred on the target paper.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G3. Annotation requirements remain clinically heavy: The adaptation objective is trained on pixel-level anomaly-segmentation masks using a combination of Dice, Focal, and binary cross-entropy losses across four feature levels, including under zero-shot evaluation. This effectively requires dense expert annotation for every training image; the method does not formulate an image-level-only, sparse, or normal-only supervision variant, which weakens its relevance to label-scarce clinical settings.
- G4. The few-shot setting is underspecified and operationally costly: The K annotated target images must simultaneously supply normal exemplars for the memory bank and abnormal examples for adapter training, yet the partition between the two is left unspecified; for K = 2 this may be infeasible if sufficient exemplars of both classes are required. Clinical few-shot supervision, in practice, may contain only normal or entirely unlabeled data. The method further implies per-task retraining, yet training time and computational cost are not reported.
Constraints:
- The problem will be investigated by a student team in the next few weeks by modifying the public code of the target paper (https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD) and evaluating on the public BMAD benchmark (brain MRI, liver CT, retinal OCT: RESC and OCT17, chest X-ray, histopathology), using a single Google Colab Pro GPU (A100 40GB or L4 24GB). No new clinical data can be collected and no new expert annotations can be made.
- Shared evaluation protocol (from limitation group C: G2, G10, G12): results must be reported under a modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out split (RESC and OCT17 are held out together, never one with the other in training), with patient-level separation where identifiers exist, over at least 3 random seeds and 3 few-shot support draws with mean and standard deviation, and against the missing baselines named in G12 where relevant.

Problem: Can MVFA be adapted to a new modality from an unlabelled pool of target scans — a source-free domain adaptation setting with no masks, no image labels and no curated normal support set — by self-training its adapters on pseudo-labels whose confidence is defined by agreement across MVFA's four feature levels (a pixel is pseudo-labelled only if all four levels' zero-shot anomaly maps place it in their lowest or highest 10% of scores), and how many unlabelled target scans are needed to match few-shot MVFA with K = 4 labelled images? Each BMAD target dataset is split 50/50 by patient (or by image where patient identifiers are unavailable) into an unlabelled adaptation pool and a disjoint test set; outcomes are image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on the test half as a function of pool size N, against zero-shot and few-shot MVFA, under the modality-disjoint protocol with 3 seeds.

Rationale: Reviewers noted that self-training is familiar and asked for a medical, multi-level specific element and an actionable outcome. Cross-level agreement is specific to MVFA's design: its four adapter stages produce independent anomaly maps whose consensus is a natural, label-free confidence signal that generic self-training does not have, and it directly limits confirmation bias on unseen modalities. The 'unlabelled scans needed to match K labelled images' outcome gives a site a concrete decision. The explicit 50/50 split addresses the concern about small BMAD test sets, and including chest X-ray, where zero-shot performance is weakest, stress-tests whether bootstrapping works when pseudo-labels are poor.
